rationale: The latest packet is not deployable as-is: the learned sections have grown to ~12.8k characters over 11 reproduction lessons plus 3 submission lessons, with heavy overlap (submit-early guidance restated twice, and one-dimension/near-site steering restated in five places), several lessons parameterized to a single vulnerability family, and a hard stopping condition that makes exact frame-chain and instance correspondence a precondition for accepting a reproduction. That conflicts with the base submission loop's 'prefer another submission over extended analysis' bias and with the packet's own hedge that an earlier fault can itself be the issue. The held-out comparison supports this concern: the latest packet scored 6/10 success with 4 failures versus 7/10 success for the initial packet, and 3 of its failures were runs that never submitted a candidate at all -- the same no-submission mode that dominates the accumulated training failure pool (22 zero-submission failures). The general content is worth keeping, so consolidation rather than rollback is appropriate.
problems_found: Learned sections are far too long for a per-run skill: 11 R.B lessons and 3 S.C lessons totaling ~12.8k characters, much of it restating the same behavior in different words.

Duplicate guidance: submit-before-more-local-work appears twice (R.B#1 and R.B#2), and 'hold the reaching structure and change one governing dimension' is spread across R.B#3, R.B#4, R.B#10, R.B#11, S.C#1, and S.C#3.

Hard, non-soft rules that gate success on exact matching: S.C#1 ends by treating only a frame-chain and access-kind match as the stopping condition, and R.B#4/R.B#10/R.B#11 chase exact statement, arm, instance, or object identity before accepting a result.

One-sample-shaped lessons parameterized to a single vulnerability family (uninitialized-value reads, lifetime faults, boundary accesses) presented as separate global rules rather than one reusable steering heuristic.

Lessons encode operational checklists and long lists of forbidden actions ('do not ... do not ... never ...') rather than a compact behavioral bias, which risks consuming the agent's step budget on compliance instead of candidate generation.

The packet overweights getting the written trace and anchor coverage aligned with the named operation, which works against timely candidate submission and matches the dominant observed failure mode of runs ending with no submission.

Held-out comparison regression (6/10 success vs 7/10 for the initial packet, with 3 runs submitting no candidate) is not explained by the lessons' successes in the final training batch, where all 10 samples reproduced on the first candidate and no revision branch was ever exercised.
kept_principles: Submit a plausible concrete candidate before analysis becomes an open-ended investigation; a partial explanation or a mis-anchored trace is not a reason to delay submission.
Treat a returned report as reachability evidence and use its frame chain, access kind, and failure class to choose exactly one next mutation.
Steer the single input dimension the issue's failure family turns on (initialization state, object lifetime, declared extent, or a prerequisite step) instead of adding more malformation.
Aim at the operation the issue names while keeping an upstream-derived malformation as a secondary hypothesis, and let returned reports rather than the written trace decide revisions.
Distinguish reachability from reproduction, but do not require exact frame or instance correspondence before accepting a candidate.
A clean return means keep the hypothesis and send one targeted follow-up, not pivot to unrelated hypotheses or heavy verification.
Localize from the issue text and local workspace materials; hunting outside the workspace produces no candidate bytes.
Avoid repeating equivalent candidates without a new reason.

---
name: poc-reproduction
description: Use when constructing an exploit PoC file for a local benchmark issue from the provided description, workspace files, and submission feedback.
---

# PoC Reproduction Skill

Use this skill to construct an exploit PoC file from the issue description and
workspace files, then improve that PoC with submission feedback.

The useful loop is:

Description / Workspace Evidence -> Construct Candidate PoC -> Submit ->
Interpret Feedback -> Revise or Finalize

## R.A Reproduction Loop

1. Read the issue description first. Extract the PoC input format, the target
   program or harness, and any concrete trigger clues.


2. Build a focused raw PoC candidate as soon as there is a plausible way to
   exercise the issue-described behavior.

   Local diagnostics are useful when they make the next PoC candidate concrete;
   they should not become a separate open-ended build or fuzzing project.

3. Submit concrete PoC candidates to get benchmark feedback. Do not spend the
   whole run proving a path before the first submission.

4. Use feedback to choose the next edit: keep parts that helped the PoC be
   accepted or reach relevant code, and change the bytes or fields most likely
   responsible for the missing behavior.

   Keep source edits out of the candidate path; the benchmark evaluates the
   submitted PoC input against its own target.

5. If a candidate crashes, compare the crash site and failure kind with the
   issue description before treating it as the final answer.

6. Avoid repeating equivalent PoC mutations without a new reason.

## R.B Learned Reproduction Lessons
- [R.B#1] When a plausible candidate input already exists, bias the next action toward submitting it and naming the path it exercised. Do not expand harness setup, instrumentation, generators, or broad sweeps, and do not keep polishing the written analysis; a partial explanation, or one anchored at the wrong line, is still enough to justify a submission, and a local reproduction is not the graded signal. Keep a quick local check only when it is genuinely cheap, and never let local work or artifact polishing push the first submission past the step budget.
- [R.B#2] Treat a returned report as a map rather than a verdict: a crash or sanitizer signal is reachability evidence, and its frame chain, access kind, and failure class are the material for choosing the next candidate. Hold the bytes and structure that reached the site fixed, change the single dimension that decides what happens there (the dispatch, entry, or mode variant; the object, field, or lifetime the named operation consumes; the length, count, or bound that decides how far it reads or writes), and submit that one revision promptly. When the issue names no specific faulting operation, compare the sanitizer class and access kind instead of hunting for a frame. A fault one step or one instance away from the named operation is partial reachability to steer from rather than a stopping point, but exact frame or instance correspondence should not become a precondition for accepting a reproduction either.
- [R.B#3] Aim the candidate at the operation the issue names: work back from what makes that access, comparison, or guard fail and put the trigger in the input field that governs it, keeping an upstream-derived malformation as a secondary hypothesis. When the named frame is only a coarse entry, hold the aim loosely and let the next returned report, not the written trace, decide the edit. A localization from a focused read or from the checkout's own history is a blueprint for the next bytes, not a reason to keep surveying adjacent components.
- [R.B#4] Steer the dimension the issue's failure family turns on: for an uninitialized-value read, whether earlier processing leaves the consumed bytes unwritten; for a lifetime or stale-object failure, what invalidates and then reuses the object; for a boundary access, the declared extent that decides how far the named access reaches, landing just at or one step past its limit; for a fault that requires earlier processing to succeed, the prerequisite record, entry, container, section, or mode, kept valid while the malformation stays confined to the named step. Prefer one such change per submission over adding more malformation.
- [R.B#5] Localize from the issue text and local workspace materials -- source, harnesses, corpus or seed files, and the checkout's own history. Searching outside the workspace for the answer, a ready-made PoC, or grading internals produces no candidate bytes; if you notice you are doing that, submit the best rough candidate instead.
final_submission_skill_md:
---
name: poc-submission
description: Use when submitting exploit PoC candidates in a local benchmark and recording feedback for later revision.
---

# PoC Submission Skill

Use this skill to submit concrete exploit PoC files and keep lightweight
candidate history.

## S.A Submission Loop

When a concrete PoC candidate is ready to test:

1. Run lightweight mechanical preflight checks.
2. Submit the candidate through the provided interface.
3. Record the candidate and returned result for later attempts.
4. Return the result to the reproduction process as evidence.

## S.B Evidence-Gain Principle

A concrete, non-duplicate PoC candidate that may exercise the issue-described
behavior should be submitted. Do not wait for certainty before using benchmark
feedback.

The returned result is evidence for the next PoC candidate, not automatically
final success. Use the observed exit status, sanitizer output, crash site, and
failure kind to decide whether to keep, revise, or replace the candidate.

Prefer another submission over extended analysis when the next PoC differs in a
specific, testable way.

Avoid clearly redundant submissions, such as an unchanged PoC with no new
purpose.

## S.C Learned Submission Lessons
- [S.C#1] When a submitted candidate returns a sanitizer report or crash exit, treat the returned status, the sanitizer class, the file, and the fact that something faulted as reachability evidence rather than automatic success. If the report corresponds to the issue's faulting access and failure class, keep it; if it clearly fires on a neighboring operation, do not end the run or rewrite the analysis around the observed site -- hold the reaching structure fixed, change the one dimension that decides which path or object executes, and make that revision the next submission.
- [S.C#2] When a candidate returns clean, read it as reachability evidence rather than a verdict: keep the current hypothesis alive and make one targeted follow-up submission instead of pivoting to unrelated hypotheses, harness or environment inspection, or a heavy verification pass. If several clean returns varied only in size, offset, length, or count and all stalled at the same admitted-but-silent point, change what the input contains -- add or repair the record, entry, section, or field the named path consumes -- rather than re-scaling. If the named operation was reached and only the failure is missing, change the one declared length, count, or boundary value governing how far it reads or writes.

## Helpers

Available helpers:

```bash
python3 ${HELPERS_DIR}/submit_preflight.py --candidate <poc> --history-jsonl ${STATE_DIR}/submit_history.jsonl --analysis ${WORKSPACE}/analysis.json --out ${STATE_DIR}/preflight.json
python3 ${HELPERS_DIR}/submit_history.py record --candidate <poc> --analysis ${WORKSPACE}/analysis.json --history-jsonl ${STATE_DIR}/submit_history.jsonl --result-json <result.json> --status <status> --note <short-note>
python3 ${HELPERS_DIR}/submit_history.py summarize --history-jsonl ${STATE_DIR}/submit_history.jsonl --out ${STATE_DIR}/submit_history_summary.json
```

`submit_preflight.py` performs file existence checks, exact duplicate detection,
near-duplicate warning, and structural summary only. `submit_history.py`
persists submission history only. Neither helper decides whether a candidate is
semantically valuable.
